newsitem.title: UKRAINE: FEATURE - Ukraine tries to reduce dependency on Russian oil.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ukraine tries to reduce dependency on Russian oil.

text.p: Ukraine, both consumer and conveyor of Russian oil, has taken its first steps towards diversifying supplies after five years of efforts aimed at reducing its dependence on its giant neighbour.
But some of the steps, such as long-term plans to buy oil from the Middle East and Caspian regions, are a long way off from making the former Soviet republic free of dependance on Russia.
"At last we have real developments instead of just words," Olexander Sverdlov, head of the transport department at the State Oil and Gas Comittee, told Reuters.
"We have reached agreements with exporters on routes proposed by Ukraine. The game has started."
But a lack of oil terminals, tanker fleets and cash, as well as resistance from Moscow, have slowed the process, and many of the plans remain on the drawing board.

"Our clumsy state apparatus has at least come close to getting alternative oil -- but it's too early to tell the band to strike up and call celebrations," said Vitaly Knyazhansky, energy commentator at the respected Den daily.
RUSSIA WOULD NOT BE HAPPY WITH ALTERNATIVE OIL
Ukraine consumes about 40 million tonnes of oil a year -- three-quarters of it imported from Russia.

Kiev's energy debt stands at $3.5 billion and some officials fear Moscow might use the arrears as a political bargaining chip in quarrels over division of the Black Sea fleet, Russian claims to the fleet's base in the Ukrainian port of Sevastopol and other disagreements over former Soviet assets.
Energy officials said Ukraine needed at least three different energy suppliers to maintain national security.
"Russia's attitude to our search for other sources is negative -- what else can you expect?" said Sverdlov. "It creates competition for the Russian oil monopoly.
"But our position is strong because not only importers but also exporters want several routes for their oil. They want this even more."
VARIOUS ROUTES PLANNED, BUT SOME DON'T EVEN EXIST
Ukraine does not want to totally give up buying oil from Russia - it just wants supplies from more than one source.
Three non-Russian options are under consideration -- not only for domestic consumption but also for the transit tariffs they will generate for Kiev if Ukraine can export more outside oil to Europe.
Last year, 53 million tonnes of Russian oil were exported across Ukraine to Western markets.
Sverdlov, who recently visited Baku with a senior energy delegation, said Azerbaijan had agreed to supply Ukraine with one million tonnes of oil this year.
The oil would be delivered by rail across Azeri and Georgian territories to the Georgian Black Sea port of Poti and then by a newly-opened ferry link to Ukraine's port of Odessa.

Ukraine could benefit when repairs and construction on a pipeline from Baku to the Georgian oil terminal Supsa is completed in 1998, Sverdlov said. It could get 29 million tonnes of Azeri oil as well as output from the 13-member international group Azerbaijan International Operating Company, and both consume and re-export the oil.
Kiev already pays nearly world prices for Russian oil and officials say it could pay the same for oil from other sources.

In addition to Azeri oil, Ukraine wants to extend the Caucasus oil corridor to Kazakhstan, where the Tengiz oil field has been developed by an international consortium led by U.S. oil giants Chevron and Mobil.
Ukraine's idea is buy some Tengiz oil for domestic use but also to help export it to world markets.

The second option foresees deliveries of Iranian and Iraqi oil by way of Turkey when construction on a planned 650 km (405 miles) pipeline from a Mediterranean oil terminal near the city of Ceyhan to Turkey's Black Sea port of Samsun is completed.

Officials said Ukraine's bid to win contracts for Iraqi oil under the United Nations' oil-for-food deal failed, and regular Iraqi exports will not take place until U.N. sanctions against Baghdad for its 1991 invasion of Kuwait are lifted.
HOPES OF FOREIGN AND PRIVATE INVESTMENT
Sverdlov said Ukraine and Turkey were conducting a joint search for the $1.8 billion project and hoping for help from European financial institutions and private investors.

Deputy Foreign Minister Kostyantyn Hryshchenko, who recently led a Ukrainian delegation to Iran, told Reuters Kiev would get up to one million tonnes of Iranian oil this year, delivered to a refinery near Odessa.
"We will have to see how our refineries deal with Iranian oil because it differs slightly from the others," he said.
Kiev also wants to collect oil from Turkish, Syrian and other Mediterannean terminals by tanker and says it would not add to traffic in the Bosphorus, something Turkey worries about.
"We are talking about small tankers; we already have an agreement with Turkey (to pass the straits)," said Hryshchenko. "The tankers will weigh 150,000 tonnes. It's okay."
AMBITIOUS PLANS, BUT A LACK OF CASH

Three years ago, Ukraine began building an oil terminal at the Black Sea port of Pivdenny near Odessa with a capacity of 40 million tonnes. But progress has been excruciatingly slow because of a lack of money.

Yuri Poluneyev, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development's director from Ukraine, said the bank was considering Kiev's request to fund one third of the $300 million project but that it was looking to award less than $100 million.

The terminal is aimed not only at Ukraine's domestic needs but at extending exports to Europe once it is connected with the Druzhba (Friendship) pipeline, which carries Russian oil to European customers via Ukraine.
Since the 1991 collapse of the former Soviet Union, Druzhba has not worked at capacity and could carry much more oil.
Ukraine could transport up to 40 million tonnes of oil from various sources to Europe on top of the 20 million tonnes transported annually through the pipeline in recent years.
To make things work Ukraine has started building a pipeline to connect the future Odessa terminal with Druzhba.
The 670 km (420 miles) link, with 40 km (25 miles) of pipes already laid, will carry oil from Odessa to Druzhba with the connection at the western town of Brody.
The plan is to export Azeri and Kazakh oil to the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Hungary and former Yugoslavia at first.
The second stage -- an extension of the pipeline to Poland -- would connect Odessa with another stretch of the Druzhba pipeline that carries Russian oil to Poland and Germany via Belarus.
Lyubomyr Bunyak, director of Ukraine's section of Druzhba, which has invested up to $30 million in the Odessa-Brody link, told Reuters Kiev had asked the EBRD to finance the pipeline.
"The completion of the Odessa oil terminal and pipeline to Brody is Ukraine's most important strategic task now," Bunyak said. "It's Ukraine's top economic and diplomatic priority."
